article_title: Why You Should Never Put a Photo on Your Resume
meta_title: Why You Should Never Put a Photo on Your Resume
meta_description: Thinking of adding a photo to your resume? Here's why it can hurt your chances — from ATS parsing issues to hiring bias — and where your photo should actually go instead.
meta_keyword: photo on resume, should you put a photo on your resume, resume photo mistake, ats resume parsing issues, resume with picture pros and cons, linkedin photo vs resume photo, resume formatting mistakes, professional resume tips

category.article_description: Expert tips and useful guidance to help you create a professional, ATS-friendly resume and improve your chances of getting hired.

contents.content:
I used to think adding a photo made my resume look more "professional." Looked good in my head — a nice headshot in the corner, polished, put-together. Then a hiring manager friend of mine actually laughed when she saw it. Not in a mean way, more like, "oh, you still do that?" That one comment changed how I look at resumes completely.

Turns out, in a lot of places — especially if you're applying to companies in the US, UK, or any multinational — a photo on your resume isn't just unnecessary. It can actually work against you. I didn't believe it at first either. Felt almost counterintuitive, like, how could a photo possibly hurt me? But once you actually sit down and think through how recruiters and hiring software work, it starts making a lot more sense.

Let's go through this properly, one reason at a time.

1. It Opens the Door to Bias (Even Unintentional Bias)

Nobody wants to admit this, but it's true — the moment a recruiter sees your face, their brain starts making judgments. Age, race, weight, whether you "look tired," whether you "look like a good fit." None of this is fair, and most recruiters aren't doing it on purpose. It's not malicious most of the time. It's just how human brains work — we form snap impressions in milliseconds, long before logic kicks in.

This is exactly why so many companies that genuinely care about fair hiring practices will strip photos out of resumes before passing them to the hiring manager. Some go even further and anonymize names too, because names can carry the same kind of unconscious bias. If a company is actively removing something from your resume before it even gets reviewed, that should tell you something about whether it was helping you in the first place.

2. Legal Risk for the Company Hiring You

This part genuinely surprises people when I bring it up. In countries like the US, including a photo can actually create legal exposure for the employer, not you. Here's the logic — if they reject you, and you happen to be, say, over 40, or belong to a visible minority group, a photo on your resume makes it much harder for them to prove in court (if it ever came to that) that the rejection had absolutely nothing to do with how you look.

Because of this, a lot of HR departments have a blanket policy: resumes with photos get flagged, sometimes discarded automatically, or the candidate gets asked to resend a version without one. Either way, you've just added an extra step of friction that nobody asked you for, and in a hiring process where attention spans are already short, friction is the last thing you want.

3. ATS Software Doesn't Know What to Do With It

Most companies today — even smaller ones — run resumes through an ATS (applicant tracking system) before a human ever opens the file. These systems are built to parse plain text. Your name, your work history, your skills section, your education. That's what they're optimized for.

Images confuse them. Sometimes the photo file breaks the formatting entirely, pushes your actual content into weird columns, or just gets ignored while quietly eating up space that could've held one more line about something you actually accomplished.

Resume Element What ATS Typically Does With It
Plain text (skills, experience, education) Reads and indexes it correctly
Photo Often ignored entirely, sometimes breaks the layout
Fancy icons or graphics Frequently causes parsing errors
Tables inside the resume itself Can scramble the reading order completely
Headers/footers with contact info Sometimes skipped by older ATS versions

If you've ever wondered why a resume that looks gorgeous in Canva gets rejected before a human even sees it — this is usually why. The visual stuff that looks great to your eyes is often invisible, or actively harmful, to the software reading it first.

4. It Takes Up Space That Should Be Selling You

A resume photo usually eats up a good chunk of real estate — space that could instead hold one more bullet point about a result you delivered, a project you actually led, a number that proves your value in a way adjectives never will. Recruiters, on average, spend something like 6 to 7 seconds on that first resume scan. Maybe a little more if something catches their eye early.

Think about what that means practically. You've got a few seconds to prove you're worth a second look. Do you want that space occupied by a photo, or by the line that says you increased efficiency by 18% or led a cross-functional team through a product launch? The math isn't close.

5. It Can Look Outdated, Even If You Don't Mean It To

Photo-on-resume used to be the norm, especially a decade or two back, and it's still completely standard practice in some countries — parts of Europe, for instance, or certain Asian markets where it's practically expected. But in a lot of modern hiring, especially tech and corporate roles in English-speaking markets, it tends to read as a little old-fashioned.

It's not a dealbreaker by itself. Nobody's going to toss your resume just because of a photo alone. But combined with other dated habits — an "Objective" statement at the top, Times New Roman font, a fax number nobody's used since 2009 — it starts to paint a picture of someone who hasn't updated their approach in a while. And that impression, fair or not, matters.

So Where Should Your Photo Actually Go?

LinkedIn. Genuinely, that's really it. Your LinkedIn photo matters a lot more than people realize — recruiters absolutely judge that one, and it should look current, approachable, and professional. People form an opinion about your LinkedIn photo in roughly the same few seconds they'd glance at a resume, so it's not like photos don't matter anywhere. They just belong somewhere else.

Where Photo Needed?
Resume No — leave it off
LinkedIn profile Yes, and keep it recent
Portfolio website Optional, depends on the field you're in
Modeling/acting resume (special case) Yes, that's just how that industry works
Email signature Optional, not a big deal either way

A Few Exceptions Worth Knowing

Like most advice, this isn't a universal rule carved in stone. There are a handful of situations where it genuinely doesn't apply:

  • Some countries — Germany, and parts of Asia in particular — still expect a photo on resumes, so it's worth checking local hiring norms before assuming the US/UK standard applies everywhere
  • Creative industries like acting, modeling, or certain performance-based roles genuinely require a photo as part of the application
  • If a job posting explicitly asks for a photo to be included, just follow the instruction, don't overthink it
  • Internal company transfers sometimes use a slightly different, more relaxed format where a photo doesn't matter either way

Outside of those specific cases though, my honest take is just leave it off. Your resume has exactly one job — get you an interview. Let your actual work history do that heavy lifting, not your headshot.

What To Do Instead

If you're used to having a photo on your resume and now feel like something's missing without it, here's what to fill that space with instead:

  • A short, specific summary line at the top — not a generic "hardworking professional seeking opportunities" line, but something that actually says what you do and what you're good at
  • One more quantified achievement from your most recent role
  • A skills section tailored to the actual job description you're applying for
  • Extra white space — believe it or not, a resume that's slightly less cramped actually reads easier and looks more confident

None of these feel as visually exciting as a nice headshot, sure. But they're doing actual work for you, which is more than a photo can say.

Did you have a photo on your resume before? Curious whether it ever came up in an interview, good or bad — drop it in the comments.

article_title: She Found Out a Colleague Earned 18% More — For the Same Job
meta_title: She Found Out a Colleague Earned 18% More — For the Same Job
meta_description: One question she didn't ask cost her 18% of her salary. Here's the exact script, research steps, and situation-based approach that actually works when the number comes up.
meta_keyword: salary negotiation script, how to negotiate salary, salary gap same job, first job salary mistake, how to ask for higher salary, salary negotiation for freshers, job offer negotiation, salary negotiation tips india, what to say salary negotiation, negotiate job offer email

category.article_description: Expert tips for career growth, job search, and professional success.

contents.content:
A cousin of mine got her first job offer last year and called me in a slight panic, not because the offer was bad, but because HR had asked, "Do you have any questions about the compensation?" and she genuinely didn't know what to say back. She ended up saying "no, it's fine," accepted the number on the spot, and found out three months later that a colleague hired around the same time, doing the same work, was earning almost 18% more. Not because that colleague was more skilled. Just because he'd asked a couple of questions she hadn't.

That's the story behind most bad salary outcomes, honestly. It's rarely about lacking skill. It's about not knowing what to say in that ten-second window when the number gets mentioned.

Why This Feels So Uncomfortable in the First Place

Most people aren't taught how to talk about money directly. Culturally, especially early in a career, asking for more can feel greedy, or like you're risking the offer altogether. That fear isn't irrational exactly, but it's usually overestimated. Companies build in negotiation room on purpose in most cases — the number offered first is rarely the absolute ceiling of what's possible, especially in mid-size and larger organizations.

The discomfort mostly comes from not having a script. Once you have a few sentences ready that don't sound aggressive or awkward, the whole interaction gets a lot less stressful.

What Actually Happens on the Other Side of the Table

It helps to know that when HR extends an offer, they've usually already got a range in mind, not a single fixed number. The number they say first is very often somewhere in the lower-to-middle part of that range, not the top of it. That's not because they're trying to shortchange anyone — it's just how budgeting works internally. Asking a reasonable, well-framed question about that number is expected, not offensive.

What actually annoys hiring managers isn't negotiation itself. It's negotiation that feels entitled, unresearched, or disconnected from the actual role. Asking for 40% more with no real basis lands very differently than asking for 10-12% more with a clear, calm reason attached to it.

A Simple Way to Actually Say It

You don't need a dramatic script. Something like this usually works fine:

"Thank you for the offer, I'm genuinely excited about this role. Based on my research and the scope of responsibilities discussed, I was hoping we could look at something closer to [X]. Is there flexibility there?"

That's it. No aggression, no apology either. It states interest, gives a reason, and asks a direct question. Most people either skip the reason (which makes it sound like a random demand) or over-apologize (which makes it sound like you don't actually believe you deserve it). This version does neither.

What to Actually Research Before That Conversation

  1. Look up salary ranges for the specific role and city, not just the job title in general — a "sales executive" in a metro city and a smaller town can have very different ranges
  2. Check what similar roles pay at 2-3 comparable companies, using sites like Glassdoor, AmbitionBox, or LinkedIn salary insights
  3. Factor in your own leverage honestly — years of experience, specific skills, certifications, or a competing offer if you actually have one
  4. Decide your real minimum beforehand, privately, so you're not deciding that number under pressure mid-conversation

Walking in with even rough numbers changes the entire tone of the conversation. It stops being "please give me more" and starts being "here's what this role typically pays, and here's where I think I fit."

What This Actually Looks Like for Different Situations

Situation Approach
First job, no experience Negotiate modestly (5-10%), focus more on learning opportunities, mentorship, and role clarity than aggressive numbers
Switching jobs with 2-4 years experience Use current salary and market data together; aim for a genuine jump (15-25%) since this is the standard reason people switch
Have a competing offer Mention it factually, without ultimatums — "I have another offer at X, but I'd prefer to join here if we can get closer to that number"
Internal promotion or raise Bring documented achievements and a clear timeline of added responsibility, not just tenure

The Part People Forget: It's Not Just the Base Number

Salary negotiation isn't only about the fixed number on the offer letter. Depending on the company, there's often room to discuss joining bonus, work-from-home flexibility, review timelines (some companies will agree to a formal review at 6 months instead of the standard 12), learning budgets, or even designation, which matters more for future job hunts than people realize. If the base number genuinely can't move due to internal policy, one of these other levers sometimes can.

When It's Actually Fine to Just Accept the First Number

Not every situation calls for negotiation. If the offer already matches or exceeds what your research showed, if it's an internship or a very early entry-level role with a fairly standard fixed structure, or if you have real reasons to prioritize joining quickly over squeezing out a few extra percent, it's completely fine to accept as-is. Negotiation isn't a moral obligation — it's a tool to use when it actually makes sense, not a box to tick out of principle.

Back to My Cousin

She's since moved to a new company, and this time, when the number came up, she paused, said something close to that script above, and got a small bump plus an agreed-upon review at eight months instead of the usual one year. Nothing dramatic. No tense back-and-forth. Just one calm, prepared question that she hadn't known how to ask the first time around.

That's really the whole shift — not becoming a different, more aggressive person, just knowing what to say in that one uncomfortable moment, so the number you start with isn't decided purely by silence.

contents.content:
A friend of mine applied to eleven jobs last month. Got exactly one callback. When she showed me the resume, nothing was technically wrong with it — no typos, decent formatting, all the right sections. But it read like it was written for nobody in particular. That's usually the real problem with resumes that don't work. Not bad grammar. Not bad design. Just nothing specific enough for anyone to remember it five minutes after reading it.

So rather than another checklist, here's how that conversation with her actually went, and what came out of it. She'd actually built her first draft using a free template from ResumeSathi, which gave her a decent starting structure — the real problem wasn't the layout, it was what she'd filled into it.

"Why isn't anyone calling me back?"

The first thing I asked her was how long she thought a recruiter actually spends looking at a resume. She guessed a couple of minutes. It's closer to ten seconds, sometimes less. I've watched someone hiring for a retail chain flip through a stack of resumes and barely pause on most of them — job title, last company, a keyword or two, next. That's the reality. Not because recruiters are lazy, but because they're often looking at forty or fifty of these in one sitting.

Once that sinks in, a lot of resume decisions start making more sense. If something important is buried in the middle of a paragraph, it's basically invisible. It has to be near the top, or it doesn't count.

Her summary line read: "Dedicated professional with strong interpersonal skills seeking growth opportunities." I asked her what she actually does. She said, "I manage a small team at a clothing store and deal with customer complaints all day." That sentence — the one she said out loud, not the one she wrote — was ten times better. We just typed that in instead.

The Numbers Problem

Her experience section had a line that said "Improved store performance." I asked, by how much? She didn't know off the top of her head, so we went digging — turned out she'd increased upsell revenue by around 14% over two quarters, something she'd genuinely done but never thought to write down as a number.

That's usually where the gap is. People do things worth measuring and then describe them like they didn't. "Improved performance" versus "increased upsell revenue 14% over two quarters" — same fact, completely different impact on a reader. You don't need a stat glued onto every single line, that gets exhausting and starts to feel forced. But wherever a real number exists, it's worth digging it out.

A Quick List of What We Actually Changed

  1. Rewrote the summary in plain spoken language instead of resume-template phrases
  2. Added actual numbers wherever she could recall or estimate them honestly
  3. Moved her most relevant retail skills higher up instead of burying them under generic ones like "hardworking"
  4. Cut an old internship from four years ago that had nothing to do with her current field
  5. Switched from a two-column layout to a single column, since she was applying through online portals that likely used ATS software

None of these took more than an evening to fix. The resume wasn't rebuilt from scratch — it was mostly the same document, just sharpened.

On Formatting, Since It Comes Up Every Time

People obsess over formatting more than they should, but a few things genuinely do matter. Stick to one or two fonts — more than that and it starts looking chaotic rather than intentional. Keep the spacing between sections consistent; uneven gaps are something readers notice without quite knowing why the page feels off. If you're applying through a company's online system, avoid heavy tables or text boxes in the resume itself, since a lot of ATS software reads those poorly and can scramble your content before a human ever sees it. And save it as a PDF unless someone specifically asks for a Word file, so the formatting doesn't shift depending on whose device opens it.

One page is usually enough if you've got under seven or eight years of experience. Past that, two pages starts to make more sense, but not before. If you don't want to fiddle with margins and spacing manually, most pre-built templates on sites like ResumeSathi already handle this part correctly, so it's one less thing to worry about.

Side by Side, in Case It Helps to See It

Before After
Dedicated professional with strong interpersonal skills Manages a 4-person retail team, focused on resolving customer complaints daily
Improved store performance Increased upsell revenue by 14% over two quarters
Responsible for handling customers Resolves 30–40 customer queries daily with consistently positive feedback
Good at multitasking Manages billing, stock checks, and customer service simultaneously during peak hours

The Part People Skip: Actually Reading It Out Loud

She'd had an old phone number sitting in her contact section for weeks. Nobody had pointed it out, and she hadn't caught it either, because she'd read that resume so many times her eyes just skipped over it automatically. That's fairly common — reading something silently and reading it out loud catch completely different kinds of mistakes. If nothing else, read the final version out loud once before sending it anywhere. It's a small habit that catches an embarrassing number of errors.

What Changed After All This

She sent out the revised version to four companies the following week. Two callbacks. Not a massive sample size, sure, but the difference wasn't the design or the font or anything cosmetic — it was that the resume finally sounded like it was written by someone specific, describing things they'd actually done, instead of a template filled in with safe, forgettable language.

That's really the whole point of a resume, if you strip away everything else. Not to impress anyone with vocabulary. Just to answer one question clearly enough that someone doesn't have to guess: can this person actually do the job. Everything else is just details in service of that one answer.

If you're starting from scratch and don't want to spend hours getting the layout right, ResumeSathi has a decent range of clean, ATS-friendly templates that take care of the structural side, leaving you free to focus on getting the actual content — the summary, the numbers, the specifics — right.

contents.content:
There's a strange gap between what career advice sounds like on paper and what actually happens once you're sitting at a desk on your first day, nodding along to instructions you don't fully understand. Most advice you get before starting a job is either too generic — "work hard, be punctual, network well" — or too specific to someone else's industry to be of much use to you. The lessons that actually matter tend to show up later, usually after you've already messed something up or sat through an awkward meeting wondering why nobody warned you about this earlier.

So instead of another list of obvious tips, here's a rundown of the things that tend to surprise people once they're actually in the middle of building a career, not just reading about one.

Your First Job Title Matters Less Than You Think

A lot of people stress over whether their first role has an impressive enough title. The truth is, five years down the line, almost nobody cares what your first designation was. What they care about is what you were actually responsible for, what you learned, and whether you can talk about it with some confidence. A slightly underwhelming title with real hands-on work will usually take you further than an inflated title where you spent most of your time waiting for someone to hand you a task.

If you're choosing between two offers and one has a fancier title but less actual responsibility, it's worth thinking twice before picking the title over the experience.

Nobody Is Going to Hand You a Roadmap

This one catches almost everyone off guard. In school and college, there's always a syllabus, a deadline, someone telling you what's expected next. Work doesn't really function that way, especially once you're past the very first few months. Managers are busy, priorities shift, and a lot of the time you're expected to figure out what needs doing before someone explicitly tells you.

This isn't a flaw in the system — it's just how most workplaces run. The people who tend to grow faster aren't necessarily the smartest ones in the room; they're often the ones who got comfortable asking questions early, tracking their own progress, and not waiting around for permission to take initiative on small things.

Feedback Feels Worse Than It Is

Getting told that something you did wasn't quite right stings, especially early on when you're still trying to prove yourself. It's easy to read criticism as a judgment on your ability rather than what it usually is — a comment on one specific piece of work. Most managers giving feedback aren't trying to make a point about your worth as an employee; they're just trying to get the actual output closer to what's needed.

It helps to separate the emotional reaction from the actual content of what's being said. Write the feedback down if you have to, sit with it for a bit, and come back to it once the initial sting has faded. Nine times out of ten, it reads a lot more reasonable an hour later than it did the moment you heard it.

Staying Too Long Can Be as Risky as Leaving Too Soon

There's a lot of advice out there warning people against job-hopping, and there's some truth to that — constantly switching jobs every few months can raise questions. But the opposite mistake happens just as often and gets talked about far less: staying in a role for years past the point where you're actually learning anything new.

If a role has flattened out — no new skills, no new responsibility, no real growth in pay or scope — comfort alone isn't a strong enough reason to stay. It's worth periodically asking yourself whether you're still growing where you are, or just familiar with where you are. Those are two very different things. Here's a rough way to check where you actually stand:

Signal Time to Stay Time to Start Looking
Learning You're still picking up new skills every few months Your day-to-day hasn't changed in over a year
Responsibility Your scope of work keeps expanding You're doing the exact same tasks as when you joined
Pay & Growth Appraisals reflect your actual contribution Raises feel more like inflation adjustments than growth
Motivation You still feel some pull toward the work You're mentally checked out most days

None of these signs alone means it's time to quit tomorrow. But if most of them start pointing the same direction for a few months in a row, that's usually not a phase — that's a pattern worth paying attention to.

Networking Doesn't Have to Feel Fake

A lot of people avoid networking because it feels transactional, like you're only talking to someone because you want something from them. But most of the useful professional relationships people build happen almost by accident — a colleague from an old job, someone you met at a training session, a senior who mentored you briefly and stayed in touch. Keeping those connections alive doesn't require constant effort; an occasional message asking how someone's doing, or congratulating them on a new role, keeps the door open without it feeling forced.

The people who end up with a strong professional network usually didn't set out to "build" one in a calculated way — they just didn't let old connections go cold.

Burnout Doesn't Always Look Like Exhaustion

Most people imagine burnout as being visibly tired all the time, but it often shows up more quietly — a growing sense of indifference toward work you used to care about, irritability over small things, or just going through the motions without really being present. It's easy to miss because it doesn't always come with an obvious low-energy day; sometimes it just comes with a slow loss of interest.

Catching it early matters more than people realize. Waiting until it turns into complete exhaustion before making changes — whether that's setting better boundaries, taking actual time off, or reconsidering the role itself — usually means a much longer recovery than if it had been addressed a few months earlier.

A few early signs worth watching for, before it snowballs into something bigger:

  • Dreading Monday starts well before Monday actually arrives, even on an otherwise normal weekend
  • Finding yourself annoyed by things that never used to bother you at work
  • Doing tasks just to get them off your plate, without much thought about doing them well
  • Feeling tired in a way that a good night's sleep doesn't really fix
  • Losing interest in conversations about work you'd usually have had opinions on

The Long Game Usually Beats the Quick Win

Early in a career, it's tempting to chase whatever looks impressive right now — the highest starting salary, the flashiest company name, the fastest promotion. Those things aren't unimportant, but they aren't everything either. A slightly lower-paying job that teaches you skills you'll use for the next decade is often worth more in the long run than a higher-paying one that leaves you exactly where you started, skill-wise, two years later.

None of this means ignoring practical concerns like salary or stability — those matter too, especially depending on where someone is in life. It just means it's worth asking not only "what does this job pay me right now" but also "what does this job teach me that I get to keep, no matter where I go next."

contents.content:
So you're staring at a blank resume template again, and somehow it still feels confusing. I get it. There are literally hundreds of resume designs floating around online right now, and half of them look like they were made for a graphic designer's portfolio, not for someone applying to an actual job. Some have sidebars, some have circular skill meters, some have photos and colored headers that take up a third of the page. And then there's the plain kind — just black text, a name at the top, a few clean sections, nothing flashy. People often assume the fancier one wins. In real hiring situations, that's usually not true.

Before picking a template, it actually helps to step back and understand that resumes aren't just "designs." They fall into a few real categories, and each one is built around a different hiring situation. Once you know which bucket you're in, choosing a layout becomes a lot less stressful.

The Four Resume Types Nobody Really Explains Properly

Most career sites throw templates at you without explaining why they exist. Here's the short version, without the jargon.

  • Chronological Resume — This is the old faithful. Work history listed newest to oldest. Recruiters are trained to scan this format fast because it's what they've seen a thousand times. If your career has been fairly linear, this is almost always the safest bet.
  • Functional Resume — Built around skills instead of a strict timeline. Good if you've had gaps, took a break, or you're switching into a completely different field and don't want your past job titles to be the first thing someone judges you on.
  • Combination Resume — A blend of both. You get a skills section up top and then a chronological work history below it. This tends to suit people with a handful of years of experience who want to highlight both.
  • Creative or Visual Resume — Heavy on design, color, icons, sometimes even illustrations. Common in design, advertising, or media roles where the resume itself is expected to show off some visual sense.

None of these is "the best" one objectively. It really depends on what job you're applying for and who's going to be reading it — a human, a hiring software, or both.

Where a Plain, No-Nonsense Layout Actually Fits

Now, the layout style we're talking about here — bold name up top, one horizontal line for email, phone, city, and website, then clean sections for Summary, Skills, Experience, and Education stacked one after another — this is basically a stripped-down chronological resume. No sidebars. No color blocks fighting for attention. No decorative graphics pretending to be relevant. Just information, laid out in the order someone would naturally want to read it.

There's a reason this style keeps showing up again and again, even though it looks "boring" compared to some templates. A huge number of companies now run resumes through Applicant Tracking Systems before a human even glances at them. These systems are notoriously bad at reading resumes with tables, multiple columns, or graphics — sometimes they scramble the text order completely or skip sections entirely. A single-column, text-first resume almost never has that problem. It just gets read the way it's meant to be read.

So while a creative resume might turn heads visually, a simple layout like this one is often the one that actually survives the first digital filter and lands in front of an actual person, which honestly matters a lot more than how it looks on a screen.

Who This Layout Actually Makes Sense For

This kind of clean, no-frills format tends to work particularly well for:

  • Retail, sales, and customer-facing roles, where clarity and quick scanning matter more than visual impression
  • Cashier, POS operator, and front-desk type positions
  • Fresh graduates or first-time job seekers who don't have a long history to fill up space with anyway
  • Operational roles — warehouse, inventory, logistics assistant positions
  • Any application submitted online through a company portal, since most of those run ATS scanning
  • People switching careers who still want something that reads clean and doesn't distract from the actual content

On the flip side, if you're applying somewhere design-heavy — say, a branding studio, a UI/UX role, or something in the creative arts — a plain layout might actually undersell you a little. In those fields, a bit of visual flair is almost part of the job requirement, since the resume is a small sample of your design sense. But for retail, sales, admin, operations, and most entry-level corporate jobs, keeping it simple usually works in your favor rather than against it.

Small Details That Make This Kind of Layout Work

What's interesting is that even a "simple" resume has small design decisions baked into it that make it easier to read. A few worth noticing:

  • The name is large and bold, so it's the very first thing anyone's eyes land on — which is exactly how it should be.
  • Contact details are squeezed into one single line instead of stacking on separate lines, which saves vertical space that can be used elsewhere.
  • Section headers are separated with a thin horizontal rule rather than a colored background, which keeps things visually calm without wasting ink or looking cluttered.
  • Skill levels are shown with small tags like Intermediate, Advanced, or Master instead of long-winded explanations, so a recruiter gets the picture in half a second.
  • Each section has a clear beginning and end, so someone skimming for ten seconds — which is genuinely how long most resumes get looked at — can still find what they need without hunting for it.

None of these choices are accidental, even though the layout looks effortless. Good simple design usually takes more thought than a busy one — it's the difference between removing everything unnecessary and never thinking about what was necessary in the first place.

Why People Still Underestimate Simple Resumes

There's a weird bias people carry when they're job hunting — they think a resume needs to "look impressive" the way a poster or an invitation card does. But a resume isn't marketing material in that sense. It's closer to a form that needs to be filled out clearly so a stranger, who has thirty other resumes to get through that same hour, can quickly figure out whether you're worth calling. Every unnecessary design element is basically friction. It slows the reader down, even by a second or two, and in a stack of applications, seconds matter more than people realize.

This doesn't mean every resume should look identical or lifeless. A little personality in the wording, a well-chosen accent color, a clean font — all of that is fine and can still make a resume feel put-together. The line is between "designed with intent" and "designed to look busy." The layout we've been talking about sits comfortably on the right side of that line.

A Small Reality Check

Here's the thing nobody likes to hear: the layout is just the container. It genuinely does not matter how clean, minimal, or well-organized a resume looks if the content inside it is vague, exaggerated, or copied word-for-word from a template example. Recruiters read hundreds of resumes and they can tell within seconds when something feels generic. Numbers should be real. Skills should reflect what you can actually do. Job descriptions should sound like they came from your own experience, not from a list of buzzwords someone else wrote.

A well-structured layout can absolutely help someone get noticed faster and get past automated filters. But at the end of the day, it's the honesty and specificity of what's written inside that gets someone an interview call. The format just makes sure that message actually reaches someone in the first place, instead of getting lost or misread before it ever gets a fair chance.

article_title: Skills vs Degree: What Matters More for Getting a Job?
meta_title: Skills vs Degree: What Matters More for Getting a Job?
meta_description: Skills or a degree — which one actually gets you hired? A practical, field-by-field breakdown to help you figure out where to invest your time.

contents.content:
Somebody asked me this the other day, half joking — "should I just drop out and learn to code instead?" I didn't have a one-line answer for them, and honestly, nobody really does. The truth sits somewhere in between, and it depends a lot more on the industry, the role, and the actual person than most advice online admits.

Still, it's worth pulling apart properly, because this question isn't going away. If anything, it's coming up more often now that self-taught developers, bootcamp grads, and certificate-holders are landing roles that used to require a specific degree on paper.

Why This Debate Even Exists

A degree used to be the default filter. No degree, no interview — that was pretty much it for a long time. But a few things have shifted that:

  • Tech and creative fields grew fast enough that formal education couldn't keep up with what the job actually required
  • Free and low-cost learning resources made it possible to build real skills outside a classroom
  • Portfolios, GitHub profiles, and project work started speaking louder than a transcript in a lot of hiring conversations
  • Some companies quietly removed degree requirements from job postings, especially for technical roles

That said, this shift hasn't touched every industry equally, which is really the whole point of this post.

Where Skills Tend to Win

In some fields, what you can actually do outweighs what your certificate says, and it's not close.

Field Why Skills Matter More Here
Software Development Employers usually just want to see working code, a portfolio, or GitHub activity
Digital Marketing Results from past campaigns say more than a marketing degree ever could
Graphic / UI Design A strong portfolio does the talking, formal design education is a bonus at best
Freelancing / Content Creation Clients care about output and reliability, not where you studied
Sales Track record and communication ability matter far more than qualifications on paper

Where a Degree Still Carries Real Weight

On the flip side, there are fields where skipping a degree basically closes the door before you even apply.

Field Why the Degree Still Matters
Medicine Legally required, no shortcut exists here regardless of skill level
Law Licensing and bar exams are tied directly to formal education
Government Jobs Eligibility criteria are usually degree-based by default
Core Engineering (Civil, Mechanical) Safety-critical work often requires certified, degree-backed knowledge
Academic / Research Roles Degrees are essentially the entry ticket, sometimes multiple of them

What Recruiters Are Actually Looking At

I've heard enough hiring managers talk about this to notice a pattern — most of them aren't choosing one over the other, they're weighing both against the role in front of them.

Hiring Factor What It Signals
Relevant Skills Can this person do the job on day one, or close to it
Degree Baseline discipline, foundational knowledge, sometimes just a filtering tool for large applicant pools
Portfolio / Past Work Proof over promises, this often overrides both of the above
Certifications A middle ground — shows initiative without needing four years
Interview Performance Can override a weak resume on either side entirely

So What Should You Actually Do?

This isn't really a "pick one" situation, no matter how the question gets framed online. A few honest points worth considering:

  • If you're aiming for a licensed profession, there's no getting around the degree, plan around that reality
  • If you're going into a skill-driven field, put your energy into building something you can actually show, not just certificates you can list
  • A degree plus strong skills will almost always beat either one alone, this isn't an either-or as often as people think
  • If you already have a degree in an unrelated field, don't assume it's wasted, transferable skills count more than people give them credit for
  • Whatever path you're on, keep building a portfolio, work samples convince people faster than any qualification does

Where I'd Land On This

Neither skills nor a degree wins this argument outright, and honestly, anyone who tells you it's a clean answer is probably trying to sell you something. What actually gets you hired is being useful for the specific role you're applying for. Sometimes that means a degree. Sometimes it means a portfolio and a willingness to prove yourself in the interview. Most of the time, it's a mix of both, plus a bit of timing and effort that no chart can really capture.

article_title: Resume vs LinkedIn Profile: What Recruiters Really Check First
meta_title: Resume vs LinkedIn Profile: What Recruiters Really Check First
meta_description: Confused about resume vs LinkedIn priority? Here's exactly what recruiters check on each, common mistakes to avoid, and how to make both work together.
meta_keyword: career advice, job search, resume tips, linkedin optimization, recruiter insights, job market trends

category.article_description: Expert tips for career growth, job search, and professional success.

contents.content:
A recruiter once told me something that kind of stuck with me for years after — she said she'd already checked my LinkedIn before she even bothered opening my resume. At the time I thought that was odd. Wasn't the resume supposed to be the main thing? Turns out no, not really, not anymore.

If you're applying for jobs right now, you already know you need both. Fine. But here's what most people get wrong — they treat these two things like they're the same document, just in two different places. They're not. A recruiter doesn't read them the same way, doesn't look for the same things, and honestly doesn't even open them in the order you'd expect.

So let's actually get into it.

Why This Mix-Up Even Happens

Most people build their LinkedIn as basically a copy of their resume. Same job titles, same "responsible for managing X" type lines, nothing that actually sounds like them. And that's the problem right there — a lot of genuinely good candidates get skipped over just because their online profile reads like a template nobody bothered to personalize.

One document filters you out. The other one decides whether someone even wants to reach out in the first place. Different jobs, different documents.

Resume vs LinkedIn — Side by Side

Factor Resume LinkedIn Profile
Main job Gets you shortlisted for one role Builds credibility over time
Format Fixed PDF, one version at a time Always changing, always live
Who's reading The hiring manager, for this job only Recruiters, old colleagues, clients, basically anyone
Tone Formal, numbers-heavy More personal, more story
Length Kept to 1-2 pages However long you want, really
Read first in 2026 Usually not Usually yes
How often updated Only when applying somewhere Constantly, almost like a running log

That "read first" row is honestly the whole point of this article, if I'm being blunt about it.

What Recruiters Actually Check on a Resume

By the time a recruiter has your resume open, they've mostly already decided you're worth a look. So now they're not reading line by line — they're scanning for a handful of specific things.

What they check Why
Keywords matching the JD ATS software filters on this before a human even sees it
Numbers, not vague claims "grew revenue 22%" lands better than "handled sales"
Progression Are you growing, or just moving sideways job to job
Layout A messy resume, fair or not, reads as a messy person
Employment gaps They'll ask about it eventually, so don't try to hide it

One thing that's changed a lot lately — most companies now run resumes through AI-assisted ATS before anyone human looks at it. And these systems aren't dumb keyword counters anymore, they actually understand context. So the old trick of jamming buzzwords everywhere doesn't really work like it used to.

What Recruiters Actually Check on LinkedIn

This part's different. There's no real checklist for LinkedIn, it's more of a gut impression thing.

What they check Why
Photo and banner People judge this in like 2-3 seconds, whether we admit it or not
Headline If it's just your job title, you're wasting the space
About section Sounds like a real person, or copy-pasted from somewhere
Activity Are you actually around, or is this account basically dead
Recommendations Someone else vouching for you carries weight
Endorsed skills Adds a layer of proof beyond what you say about yourself
Mutual connections Trust builds faster when there's already some overlap

Something a lot of job seekers don't realize — recruiters are now leaning on LinkedIn's own AI search and summary features to shortlist people before sending a single message. So if your profile's thin or hasn't been touched since 2021, you could get filtered out of a role you never even knew existed.

Don't Make Them Twins

I know this sounds like it goes against the "keep everything consistent" advice you've probably heard a hundred times. But consistency just means the facts line up — titles, dates, companies. It doesn't mean the writing has to be identical.

Resume version:

"Led a team of 6 to deliver a product redesign that cut customer complaints by 30%."

LinkedIn version:

"Complaints kept piling up that quarter and at some point I just couldn't keep ignoring it. Grabbed five people from the team, we tore apart the user flow from scratch — took about three months, a lot of it messier than I'd like to admit. But by the end complaints were down 30%, and it's still one of the projects I bring up when people ask what I'm proud of."

Same achievement, told two different ways, for two different audiences. Both are true. Both work.

Mistakes People Are Still Making

  • Resume photo (or worse, LinkedIn photo) that's basically five years out of date
  • Sending the identical resume to every single application, no tailoring at all
  • LinkedIn headline that's literally just your job title and nothing else
  • Never touching the "Open to Work" settings, so you're invisible to recruiter search
  • Ghost profile — zero posts, zero comments, nothing for months on end
  • Skipping recommendations because "they're not that important" (they are, now more than ever)

The Way I'd Sum This Up

Your resume is answering one question: can this person actually do the job. Your LinkedIn is answering a slightly different one: do I want to talk to this person, and can I trust what they're telling me.

There's more competition than ever right now, a lot of it AI-assisted applications flooding every posting. Which honestly makes the human stuff stand out more, not less — real stories, actual numbers, a personality that comes through instead of a generic template.

Before You Hit Apply

  • Resume actually tailored to this job, not the same one you send everywhere
  • LinkedIn headline says more than just your title
  • At least a couple of recent recommendations up
  • Photo's current, looks like you look now
  • Resume and LinkedIn facts match, even if the tone doesn't
  • You've posted or commented on something in the last month

Get this right and you stop being just another name in the pile.

Curious — does anyone actually check your resume first these days, or is it LinkedIn every time? Let me know in the comments.

I get asked this a lot — "which resume template should I actually use?" And honestly, there's no single right answer. It depends on what job you're going for, how much you want to show off visually, and whether the company you're applying to even bothers reading past the ATS screening. One template that a lot of people gravitate toward lately has a dark header, a round profile photo up top, skill bars running down the side, and a two-column body underneath it. That's the one I want to talk about here.

If you've seen it before and wondered whether it's worth using, or you're just trying to figure out if it fits your field, this should clear things up.

Breaking Down the Layout

The template is really just two zones stitched together. Nothing fancy, but it's laid out in a way that makes sense once you see it in front of you.

Section Where It Sits What Goes In It
Header Full-width, top Name, designation, location, phone, email, website
Left Sidebar Left column Skills with progress bars, Languages, Social Links, Hobbies
Main Content Right column Profile Summary, Work Experience, Internships, Education, Certifications

What I like about this setup is that it gives you room to include the extra stuff — languages, hobbies, social links — without it feeling like you're cramming things into a corner just to fit them in.

What Actually Sets It Apart

A few small design choices make this template stand out from the usual plain-text resume:

  • Skill bars next to each listed skill — instead of just naming a skill, you can show roughly how good you are at it (Intermediate, Proficient, Advanced, that sort of thing)
  • A dotted timeline running through Work Experience, Internships, and Certifications, so it reads a bit like a story instead of a list
  • One accent color used consistently across headers and icons — small detail, but it makes the resume look put-together rather than thrown together
  • A proper spot for social links, which honestly gets left out of a lot of templates even though recruiters do check LinkedIn and GitHub

Who Should Actually Go For This One

Not every template works for every job, and this one's no exception. Some fields respond well to a bit of visual flair, others really don't.

Candidate Type Good Fit? Why
Retail / Sales Professionals Yes The skill bars make your strengths easy to scan at a glance
Freshers / Students Yes Internships and education actually get proper visibility instead of being buried
Designers / Creative Roles Yes The layout itself doubles as a small demonstration of design sense
Corporate / Finance Roles Not really These industries usually expect something more conservative and text-heavy
Senior Management Roles Not really Timeline-style templates tend to read as junior to mid-level

Now, About ATS — Will It Even Get Read?

This is the part people worry about most, and fair enough. A resume can look great and still get chewed up by an applicant tracking system if it's not built carefully.

Element ATS-Safe? Note
Two-column layout Mostly Older ATS software can occasionally scramble the reading order
Skill progress bars Somewhat risky Type out the actual skill level in words too, don't rely on the bar alone
Icons for contact info Usually fine Just make sure the text sits right next to the icon, not inside it
Profile photo Depends Normal practice in India, but some international recruiters prefer no photo at all

If the company you're applying to is a large corporate setup, it doesn't hurt to keep a plainer, single-column resume on standby too. Better safe than filtered out before a human even looks at it.

A Few Things Worth Doing (and Avoiding)

Some of this is common sense, but it's easy to overlook once you're deep in template customization mode:

  • Keep the skills section tight — only what's actually relevant to the role you're applying for
  • Add real numbers to your work experience wherever you can, even something like "grew monthly sales by 10%" changes how a line reads
  • Stick to professional social links only, this isn't the place for a personal Instagram
  • Don't try to fit every section you can think of, a resume with too much going on stops being readable
  • Don't guess at your skill bar levels just to look good, recruiters notice inconsistency between what you claim and how you answer in an interview
  • Keep certification and work dates in one consistent format throughout

Timeline Template vs a Plain One — Side by Side

Factor Timeline Template Simple/Minimal Template
Visual Appeal High Lower
ATS Safety Medium High
Best For Retail, creative, entry-level roles Corporate, government, traditional industries
Customization Options High — colors, bars, icons Limited
Recruiter Scan Time Fast, guided by visuals Fast, but plainer

Where I'd Land On This

If you're in retail, sales, design, or you're a fresher still building out your work history, this template genuinely does a good job of making a thin resume look complete and a strong one look even better. But if you're eyeing a corporate or finance role, or applying somewhere known for being conservative about hiring formats, I'd lean toward something simpler instead.

At the end of the day, the best template isn't the one that looks the most polished on screen — it's the one that gets your actual experience across clearly, without getting in its own way.

contents.content:
Have you ever felt that everyone else is moving forward in their career while you still feel confused about your future? This feeling is more common than you might think, whether you're a fresher or someone with five years of experience. A successful career doesn't require a perfect plan. It requires making small, consistent decisions in the right direction. In this post, we'll look at practical ways to make better career decisions.

Why career confusion happens

Most people feel stuck in their careers because of these:

  • They don't know their actual strengths.
  • They choose safe option and ignore the actual interest.
  • Family or society pressure ends up driving major decisions.
  • They stop upgrading skills after getting a job.

If any of these points sound familiar, you're not alone. Many people face the same challenges.

5 practice steps for career planning

Step What to Do Time Needed
1. Self-Assessment Write down your skills, interests, and values, then analyze them honestly 1-2 weeks
2. Market Research Check the demand and growth potential of your target field 1 week
3. Skill Gap Analysis Compare your current skills against what the role actually requires 3-4 days
4. Build an Action Plan Plan courses, certifications, or projects to close the gap 1 week
5. Execute and Review Track progress every few months and adjust course Ongoing

This process not work perfectly in first try because career growth is rarely a straight line.

Key Skills Across Different Career Fields

Field Core Technical Skills Essential Soft Skills
Software Development Coding, Debugging, System Design Problem-solving, Patience
Digital Marketing SEO, Content, Analytics Tools Creativity, Communication
Design (UI/UX) Wireframing, Figma, Prototyping Empathy, Attention to detail
Sales & Business Dev CRM Tools, Negotiation Confidence, Listening skills
Government/Sarkari Jobs Subject Knowledge, Exam Strategy Discipline, Consistency
Teaching/EdTech Subject Expertise, Digital Tools Patience, Explaining skills

Technical skills are important, but strong communication, teamwork, and problem solving skills often help people grow faster in their careers.

Common Resume and Interview Mistakes

A lot of candidates lose out on good opportunities because of small, avoidable mistakes.

Mistake What It Causes Fix
Sending the same generic resume everywhere Recruiters don't see relevance to the role Customize your resume for each job
ATS-unfriendly formatting Resume gets rejected by the system before a human sees it Use a simple, clean, ATS-friendly format
Giving memorized, rehearsed answers Comes across as inauthentic Share real examples and personal stories
Not following up after interviews Recruiter simply forgets you Send a short, polite thank-you email
Avoiding salary discussions You end up accepting a lower package Do market research and negotiate confidently

Looking for an ATS-friendly resume? Try our free ATS Resume Checker and Resume Builder. Click here

The Most Underrated Career Skill

  • Share work-related updates or insights on LinkedIn regularly
  • Leave thoughtful comments on posts from people in your industry
  • Join alumni groups and professional communities
  • Attend events or webinars, even the online ones
  • Stay in touch with colleagues and classmates

A Realistic Career Growth Timeline

Many people expect quick results, but career growth usually takes time.

Time Period What to Expect
0-1 Year In learning phase, focus on building a solid foundation
1-3 Years Skills sharpen and confidence starts building
3-5 Years Specialization and leadership opportunities start opening up
5+ Years Clear direction and stability in your career path

Do's and Don'ts to Keep in Mind

Do:
  • Learn at least one new skill or concept every month
  • Keep your portfolio or resume updated
  • Actively seek feedback and act on it
  • Treat financial planning as part of career planning
Don't:
  • Fall into the comparison trap
  • Don't choose a job based only on salary also choose accordign to career growth opportunity.
  • Stop learning once you land a job
  • Don't ignor burnout,break is also important.

Final Thoughts

Your career is not a race. Everyone grows at their own pace. It's a continuous journey where every step teaches you something new. Don't compare your joourney with another because every one have different mindset and starting point.
